analysis.one_liner: Bars doctors from referring patients to health businesses they or their families own, and from billing for those services.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 1992 by Senator Brock Adams with two Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited doctors from sending patients to laboratories, imaging centers, physical therapy clinics, or other health businesses in which the doctor or an immediate family member had a financial stake, with a list of exceptions for things like in-office services, HMOs, rural providers, and publicly traded stock. Patients and insurers could refuse to pay bills stemming from a prohibited referral, and repeat violators faced fines of up to $15,000 per referral, loss of laboratory certification, or exclusion from Medicare. It also required health entities to disclose which doctors own them, and restricted ancillary providers from billing anyone other than the patient who received the service.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and everyone who pays for health care — individuals, private insurers, and Medicare — gain protection from treatment decisions driven by a doctor's investment rather than the patient's need. People who paid for such services could sue to recover the payment with attorney's fees, and insurers gained the right to deny claims tied to prohibited referrals.

how_it_helps.text: Doctors and their immediate family members could no longer refer patients to health entities in which they held ownership or investment interests or had compensation arrangements, outside a defined list of exceptions [S2][S3].
No patient, insurer, or other payor could be required to pay for services furnished through a prohibited referral, and anyone who collected on such a bill would be liable to refund it [S2][S3].

Health entities would have to disclose their ownership arrangements, including the names of physicians with investment interests, to the Secretary of Health and Human Services and to any payor on request [S3].

Repeated violators faced civil fines of up to $15,000 per service or referral, up to $100,000 for schemes to route referrals around the ban, suspension or revocation of laboratory certification, and exclusion from Medicare [S2][S3].
Anyone who paid for services furnished under a prohibited referral could sue in federal court to recover the payment plus attorney's fees [S3].

The bill also barred ancillary providers — labs, imaging, equipment, and physical therapy — from billing anyone other than the patient, closing a channel through which third parties were billed for services they never ordered [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Physicians and their families with ownership stakes or compensation arrangements in laboratories, imaging centers, durable medical equipment suppliers, and physical therapy clinics would lose the ability to profit from referring their own patients to those businesses. Providers would also face new ownership-disclosure and claim-identification paperwork.
analysis.who_pays_short: Physicians invested in labs, imaging, and clinics

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed substantial new paperwork on health providers: every claim would have to name the referring physician and his identification number, and every entity would have to make ownership information available to the government and to payors [S3].

Enforcement leaned partly on insurers, who would have to include a no-payment clause in their policies and report patterns of violating claims to the Secretary within 60 days, though the bill explicitly did not require them to audit individual claims [S3].

The prohibition was broad — covering any health or health-related item or service and all payors, not just Medicare — and critics could argue that even with its many exceptions, compliance would be difficult for legitimate arrangements like group practices and small rural facilities, though the bill included specific carve-outs for rural providers, ambulatory surgery centers, and physician-owned hospitals meeting a 60 percent physician-ownership threshold [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: patients and payors stop funding care chosen for the doctor's investment return rather than the patient's need, at the cost of compliance paperwork for providers and some complexity in policing the many exceptions. The exceptions were broad — in-office ancillary services, group practices, HMOs, publicly traded securities, rural providers, ambulatory surgery centers, and physician-owned hospitals meeting ownership thresholds — which narrowed the bill's reach considerably but also made it workable for legitimate arrangements. The enforcement tools (denial of payment, civil fines, private lawsuits, Medicare exclusion) were real, though proving violations would fall on the Secretary and payors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-August 1992, read twice, and sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which took no further action before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Brock Adams introduced the bill on August 12, 1992, for himself along with Senators Bingaman and Metzenbaum, all Democrats [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and no floor vote ever occurred; the bill's action history ends with the referral [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died, as bills do when a Congress expires without action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians with financial stakes in laboratories, imaging centers, and therapy clinics were better off, since they kept the freedom to refer patients to businesses they owned and bill insurers and Medicare for the resulting services. The committee that never acted on the bill also avoided taking a recorded position on the issue.

for.name: Sen. Brock Adams
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill on August 12, 1992.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Referred committee; the bill's only stop after introduction
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 12, 1992 and took no action — no markup, no report, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Physician-investors in health facilities and organized medicine
against.role: Physicians with ownership in labs, imaging centers, and clinics
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on physician self-referral during this era, an opposition widely reported in coverage of the 1992 self-referral debate.

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no party split was ever measured on the floor.

industries.industry: Physician-owned health facilities (labs, imaging, physical therapy, medical equipment)
industries.note: These businesses depended on referrals from physician-owners; the bill would have cut off billing for services furnished through prohibited referrals. Patients and insurers currently pay for services selected partly to feed the owner's investment, so the industry's interest ran against theirs.

Labs would gain legitimate volume but lose business from physician-investor referrals, and could face suspension or revocation of their certification for violations. Their interest was in keeping referral revenue flowing, which the bill would have curtailed.

Insurers would gain the right to deny claims tied to prohibited referrals, refund liability from anyone who collected improperly, and a reporting duty for violation patterns — but no obligation to audit individual claims. Their savings would flow to premiums and the public's costs would fall.

The bill carved out an exception allowing physicians to keep ownership stakes in hospitals where at least 60 percent of physician-owners perform services there, locking in physician-owned hospitals even while restricting other self-referral arrangements.
